strengths: Well-motivated benchmark addressing an important gap in evaluating 3D geometric reasoning of foundation models using mathematically well-defined polyhedra with clear ground truth

Comprehensive, high-quality dataset combining 224 diverse polyhedra (8 categories) with both synthetic renderings and hand-constructed real models, multiple viewpoints, and varied environmental conditions
Multi-faceted evaluation design with four complementary tasks (reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, classification) that probe different dimensions of geometric understanding
Thorough empirical evaluation across multiple recent models (Shap-E, SF3D, OpenLRM, CLIP, DINO, DINOv2, frontier VLMs) systematically revealing limitations
Strong qualitative analysis of VLM failure modes identifying systematic errors in face geometry, convexity, and compound structure recognition
Clear presentation, informative visualizations, and practical grounding through both synthetic and real-world data
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: benchmark creation only without proposing new models, training approaches, or evaluation techniques; evaluation methods (linear probing, zero-shot classification) are standard practice

3D reconstruction evaluation is superficial: only 3 shapes tested, only 3 models evaluated, no quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, IoU, etc.), purely visual assessment with small hard-to-interpret renderings, no ablations or complexity analysis

Mental Rotation Test lacks rigor: hard split pairs selected manually with vague criteria, only 6 examples shown, no human baseline for comparison, near-chance performance could reflect task difficulty rather than model limitations

Symmetry detection task limitations: only 3 symmetry types tested, Johnson solids excluded reducing scope, near-saturation accuracy (93%) suggests models may exploit 2D cues rather than true 3D understanding, no learned representation analysis or ablations

Dataset inconsistencies: claimed 224 polyhedra but Table 1 sums to 238 (unexplained discrepancy), incomplete attribution for physical models, unclear exact wild image composition, ground truth validation procedure not documented

Missing systematic analysis: no ablation studies on shape complexity, domain shift factors, viewpoint effects, rendering parameters; no per-category performance analysis; no investigation of which visual features drive predictions

VLM evaluation design issues: simple generic prompt may not effectively probe geometric understanding, frontier models not designed for geometry tasks, only 4 models tested, limited qualitative error analysis (4 examples), unclear model codenames vs. released versions

Reproducibility concerns: dataset availability claimed but with placeholder link, physical model construction details redacted/incomplete, scattered hyperparameter justification, linear probe training details incomplete

Insufficient experimental rigor: no error bars/confidence intervals/significance tests, no human performance benchmarks (critical for MRT and classification), no simple geometric baselines for comparison, no statistical analysis of result variability
Somewhat expected findings: models trained on 2D images struggling with 3D geometry is not surprising, no proposed solutions offered, limited scientific insight beyond benchmark contribution

strengths: Novel and well-curated dataset with comprehensive polyhedral coverage (224 shapes across 8 categories with precise mathematical definitions enabling unambiguous ground truth)
Multi-faceted evaluation covering reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, and zero-shot classification, probing different dimensions of geometric understanding
Strong combination of synthetic and real-world images with detailed physical construction from paper models, adding realistic variability
Clear, well-motivated presentation with good mathematical foundations for the choice of polyhedra as evaluation primitives
Comprehensive model coverage across reconstruction methods (Shap-E, Sf3D, OpenLRM), vision models (9+ encoders), and frontier VLMs (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT)
Valuable qualitative analysis in Section 4.4 showing systematic failure modes of VLMs (e.g., confusing component shapes, misidentifying face geometry)
weaknesses: Missing quantitative metrics for key experiments: monocular 3D reconstruction results (Table 2) are purely visual with no quantitative evaluation (Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score); without numbers, degree of failure is unclear

No human baseline performance reported despite extensive evaluation—critical for understanding if model failures are expected or surprising; MRT hard split lacks inter-rater agreement for pair selection

Shallow analysis of failure modes: paper shows models fail but provides limited mechanistic understanding of why or how to improve; minimal investigation of whether pre-training distribution, model scale, or architecture explains reconstruction failures
Manual pair selection for MRT hard split (Table 4) is subjective without validation; unclear how many pairs exist, their distribution, or sensitivity to selection bias
Incomplete experimental design: Johnson solids excluded from symmetry detection and MRT due to 'ambiguities from viewing angles'—weakens generalizability claims; justification is insufficient

Limited scope of baseline comparisons: only 3 reconstruction models, 4 VLMs, and 9 vision models tested; no comparison to classical geometric reasoning methods or ablations on model architecture/training
Synthetic rendering uses simple diffuse shading without complex illumination—may not match real image diversity sufficiently for train-on-synthetic-test-on-wild conclusions
No error analysis correlating shape complexity (face count, symmetry order, convexity) to performance degradation—missed opportunity for systematic insights
Missing ablation studies: no analysis of dataset size effects, training data composition, or contribution of individual geometric properties to model failures
Weak actionable insights for future work—paper diagnoses problems but offers limited guidance on solutions (architectural changes, training procedures, data requirements needed for improvement)

strengths: Novel, well-motivated dataset with 224 carefully selected polyhedra providing systematic variation in geometric complexity and symmetry—polyhedra are ideal for evaluation due to well-defined mathematical properties and clear ground truth

Comprehensive multi-faceted evaluation across four complementary tasks (reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, classification) with multiple model types, providing thorough assessment of geometric reasoning

High-quality dataset construction with both synthetic renderings (using Mitsuba PBR) and real-world photographs (physical paper models in varied conditions), enabling both controlled and naturalistic evaluation

Systematic identification of failure modes with detailed qualitative analysis, revealing consistent gaps in current state-of-the-art models' geometric reasoning despite strong performance on standard benchmarks

Clear presentation and careful documentation, with promising finding that DINOv2 achieves 93% accuracy on 4-fold symmetry detection despite being trained only on synthetic data, suggesting foundation models implicitly capture 3D structure
Dataset will be publicly available, enabling future research and providing lasting value to the community; benchmark is well-designed to facilitate continued progress
Well-grounded in cognitive science literature (Mental Rotation Test, symmetry perception research) providing principled evaluation framework beyond standard computer vision metrics
weaknesses: Limited depth of mechanistic analysis—paper identifies what models fail at but provides insufficient investigation into why, missing opportunities for understanding what representations enable symmetry detection but not shape differentiation

Reconstruction evaluation relies only on qualitative visual results without quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, F-score, IoU, etc.), making systematic comparison and progress tracking difficult; only 3 representative shapes evaluated in detail

Mental rotation hard split construction appears somewhat arbitrary with limited justification for pair selection and no inter-rater agreement or systematic difficulty assessment; Johnson solids excluded due to unexplained 'viewing ambiguities'
Symmetry detection evaluation covers only 3 symmetry types (missing important ones like 3-fold and reflection symmetries) and uses linear probing which may not fully capture model capabilities
VLM evaluation limited to single simple prompt without exploring prompt engineering, few-shot variants, or comparison between synthetic and wild image performance; missing human performance baseline
Statistical analysis is minimal—no error bars, confidence intervals, significance tests, or investigation of performance variance across shape categories and model sizes

Real-world images limited to single material (paper) and not all 224 shapes have physical models; preprocessing (center crop, background removal) may oversimplify real-world scenarios and scenarios realistic use

No actionable insights or proposed solutions—paper identifies geometric reasoning gaps but provides no exploration of how to improve models, no fine-tuning experiments, and limited guidance on architectural or training requirements

Generalization questions unaddressed—no investigation of whether findings transfer to non-polyhedral shapes or broader geometric domains; no analysis of how performance scales with model capacity or training data

Reproducibility concerns including sparse paper model construction details, no mention of evaluation code, incomplete specification of frontier model prompts/parameters, and some critical details relegated to supplementary material

strengths: Well-motivated dataset design with clear mathematical ground truth: polyhedra provide unambiguous evaluation criteria via symmetry groups and geometric categories
Comprehensive and hierarchical shape coverage spanning 224 polyhedra from simple (Platonic) to complex (nonconvex compounds), enabling systematic complexity analysis
Dual-modality data collection combining controlled synthetic (Mitsuba) and naturalistic real-world (paper models in diverse environments) images

Thorough multi-faceted evaluation across diverse model types (12+ encoders, 4 frontier VLMs, 3 reconstruction methods, geometry-native models) and task types (reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, classification)

Rigorous experimental methodology including 5-fold cross-validation, proper class imbalance handling, hard/easy splits with human baseline (42 participants), and careful metric selection (balanced accuracy)

Concrete, non-obvious findings revealing systematic failures: SOTA reconstruction methods fail on basic shapes; symmetry detection success (93%) doesn't transfer to mental rotation or classification; explicit 3D geometry doesn't help geometry-native models
Systematic qualitative error analysis identifying specific failure patterns (confusing convexity, hallucinating faces, conflating compounds with stellations) with actual model reasoning shown
Clear writing, informative visualizations, and thorough documentation make the paper accessible and reproducible
weaknesses: Unclear real-world significance: connection between polyhedra performance and real-world 3D reasoning is not empirically established; authors acknowledge requiring 'further empirical study' to establish correlation with arbitrary organic shapes, weakening claimed importance

Limited scope for reconstruction evaluation: only 3 shapes tested (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) across 3 methods without systematic quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, mesh evaluation); insufficient for drawing strong conclusions

Mental rotation test design concerns: 'hard split' criteria not clearly specified; massive performance drop from easy (~95%) to hard (~65%) suggests calibration issues; no ablation on difficulty factors or human-model task alignment

Symmetry detection incomplete: Johnson solids excluded 'due to ambiguities,' weakening generality; limited ablation on why DINOv2 succeeds while others fail; no analysis of which symmetries are intrinsically harder

Zero-shot classification may not probe understanding effectively: single prompt 'What is the name?' may be suboptimal; CoT/multi-view yield only marginal gains, suggesting prompting issues rather than fundamental limits; no evaluation of whether models identify geometric properties correctly despite wrong classification
Dataset availability unconfirmed: paper states 'GIQ is publicly available at [blank]' with no URL, preventing verification and reproducibility
Incomplete real-world coverage: wild images only include subset of 224 shapes; real evaluation limited to Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, and 48/92 Johnson solids

Limited mechanistic insights: paper identifies failures but lacks understanding of underlying causes (which representation dimensions encode geometry? why doesn't explicit 3D help?); no investigation of potential solutions or design principles for improvement

Missing ablations and analyses: no breakdown of performance vs. shape complexity; no analysis of preprocessing impact (background removal for reconstruction); limited ablation on task design choices; no cross-task correlation analysis
Statistical rigor gaps: most results lack confidence intervals or significance tests; no error bars on main results (Figures 3-4); human study with 42 participants is reasonable but could be larger

strengths: Well-motivated dataset design using polyhedra with unambiguous mathematical ground truth and hierarchical complexity
Comprehensive experimental coverage evaluating diverse model categories (reconstruction, encoders, VLMs, geometry-native models) across four distinct tasks
Rigorous evaluation methodology including human baselines (42 participants), 5-fold cross-validation, and both synthetic and real-world image variants
Clear documentation of concrete failure modes with qualitative analysis revealing systematic errors (convex/concave confusion, hallucinated faces, compound misidentification)
Inclusion of real paper models in natural settings tests robustness to real-world variability beyond controlled synthetic rendering
weaknesses: Narrow scope exclusively focused on polyhedra with unvalidated generalization claims to complex real-world scenes; authors acknowledge the need for 'further empirical study' to establish correlation with arbitrary organic shapes
Limited technical novelty; contributions are primarily dataset-focused using standard methods (linear/non-linear probing, zero-shot evaluation), insufficient for top-tier venues

Reconstruction experiments critically underdeveloped: only 3 shapes evaluated with qualitative results only, no quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, normal consistency, etc.) preventing rigorous failure analysis

Ambiguous interpretation of key results: 93% symmetry detection accuracy suggests models encode geometry well, but paper frames as failure; distinction between implicit and explicit reasoning never rigorously defined

Mental Rotation hard split construction lacks transparency in how 'geometrically similar' pairs were selected; results approach chance level suggesting domain gap rather than geometric reasoning failure

Zero-shot classification relies on oversimplified prompting ('What is the name of this polyhedron?'); CoT and multi-view improvements dismissed without thorough investigation; errors may reflect named entity recognition rather than geometric reasoning
Critical reproducibility issues: dataset URL is blank in paper; missing quantitative metrics, rendering parameter details, and implementation hyperparameters for probes
Limited actionable insights for practitioners; mentions CoT training data generation in conclusion without concrete implementation, validation, or proposed model improvements
Missing statistical rigor: no confidence intervals for most results; some findings near chance level discussed without investigating stability; only human study reports standard deviation
Geometry-native models (LLaVA-3D, ShapeLLM, PointLLM) underexplored despite availability of explicit 3D structure; unclear why they fail to outperform 2D pretrained models

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark using polyhedra with precise mathematical ground truth, enabling systematic evaluation of geometric reasoning with controlled complexity variation
Comprehensive dataset construction: 224 shapes with both synthetic (20 Mitsuba views) and extensive real-world images (40+ per shape with indoor/outdoor variation)

Multi-faceted experimental evaluation covering four complementary tasks (reconstruction, symmetry detection, mental rotation, classification) that probe different dimensions of geometric understanding
Strong experimental methodology including proper 5-fold cross-validation, human baseline comparison (showing 68% of humans outperform best model), and systematic ablations (CoT, multi-view inputs)
Clear and significant findings revealing systematic gap between implicit geometric understanding (strong symmetry detection) and explicit reasoning (poor MRT and classification performance)
Excellent presentation with well-motivated introduction, clear geometric preliminaries, and informative visualizations that make polyhedra taxonomy accessible
High reproducibility standards with promise of public dataset release and detailed experimental specifications
weaknesses: Limited scope restricted to polyhedra—a single artificial geometric class with perfect forms and axis-aligned properties; generalization to arbitrary organic shapes is assumed but unvalidated and unempirically studied

Reconstruction evaluation critically lacks quantitative metrics (no Chamfer distance, Hausdorff distance, IoU); only qualitative visual results on 3 examples prevents rigorous assessment of this major claim

Limited analysis of failure causes: paper documents that models fail but doesn't investigate root causes (training distribution shift? missing 3D priors? architectural limitations?), reducing actionability

Methodological concerns: hard mental rotation split selection criteria vague and potentially unfair; linear/non-linear probing conflates statistical correlation with true understanding, evident from trivial-to-hard split performance cliff

Asymmetric wild image coverage: not all 224 shapes photographed; only subsets (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, ~48 Johnson) have real images, limiting robustness claims and synthetic-to-real gap analysis

Primarily diagnostic rather than prescriptive: paper excels at showing failures but offers minimal guidance on solutions; mentions 'scale insufficient without mathematically generated data' without systematic testing
Dataset has very small categories (Platonic: 5 shapes; Kepler-Poinsot: 4) limiting generalization claims within polyhedra taxonomy itself
Unfair comparison of geometry-native models (LLaVA-3D, ShapeLLM, PointLLM) which are tested with images rather than their native 3D representations (point clouds, 3D models)
